passage:
Social science teacher's note, Class 10:
Ahead of the local elections, I asked students to bring one political claim they'd seen online. Pema brought a forwarded image claiming a candidate had built "100 new schools." Abhinav said it was obviously true because many people had shared it. I asked them to check: where did the number come from? Pema found the district education website listed twelve new schools in five years. Abhinav was quiet, then said, "So someone just made it up?" Pema said maybe they counted repairs. We discussed how elected councils decide on schools and how citizens can ask for records.
Next step: the class will write questions for a candidates' public meeting. Pema has volunteered to lead.

qa.q: How many new schools did the district education website list?
qa.a: It listed twelve new schools in five years.

qa.q: What does Abhinav's quiet moment suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Abhinav was surprised and a bit unsettled to find that something widely shared wasn't accurate.

qa.q: What did the teacher's approach teach well?
qa.a: Asking students to trace where a number came from and connecting it to how councils work taught them to check claims instead of trusting shares.

qa.q: How might a candidate see students' questions at the public meeting?
qa.a: They might be impressed, or uncomfortable, since informed questions based on real records are harder to answer with slogans.

grounding: A teacher's note shows teens checking a political claim against public records and learning how local governance works.

passage:
Wednesday
Today in civics class we did a mock election. Afreen and I were in different "parties" and had to make posters. Mine said our party would give free laptops to everyone. The teacher asked, "How will you pay for it?" I had no idea 😅
Afreen's party promised better bus routes, and she had actually worked out which roads need them. She won.
At home, Papa was watching the news and a leader said something big about jobs. I asked, "How will they pay for it?" Papa laughed and said, "Good question." I still don't get how budgets work, but I'm going to ask Afreen. She seems to know.
Pema

qa.q: What did Pema's party promise?
qa.a: Pema's party promised free laptops to everyone.

qa.q: How did Pema feel when the teacher asked how Pema would pay for it?
qa.a: Pema felt caught off guard and a bit embarrassed, with no idea at all.

qa.q: How is Pema starting to read news more critically?
qa.a: Pema is asking how big promises will be paid for, the same question that exposed the weakness in Pema's own poster.

qa.q: How might Afreen see the mock election?
qa.a: She probably enjoyed it and felt her careful planning paid off, and may be happy to explain budgets to Pema.

grounding: A teen's diary shows Pema learning through a mock election to question political promises.

Nikita: did u see the video about the voting machines being hacked??
Kalyani: which one
Nikita: the one everyone's forwarding. says the whole election is fake
Kalyani: who made it
Nikita: idk some channel
Kalyani: hmm. my mausi was a polling officer last year. she said machines are checked and sealed in front of party agents
Nikita: oh
Nikita: so the video is wrong?
Kalyani: maybe or maybe not, but it doesn't show any proof. just a guy shouting
Nikita: true 🤔
Kalyani: we could check the election office website
Nikita: ok let's do it at lunch tmrw
Nikita: I almost forwarded it to the family group 😬
Kalyani: lol glad u didn't

qa.q: What did Kalyani's mausi do last year?
qa.a: She was a polling officer.

qa.q: What does Nikita's "I almost forwarded it" suggest about Nikita's feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Nikita is a little embarrassed and relieved, realising how close Nikita came to spreading an unproven claim.

qa.q: What did Kalyani do that others could copy?
qa.a: Kalyani asked who made the video, noticed it had no proof, and suggested checking an official source instead of forwarding.

qa.q: How might Nikita's family have reacted if the video had been forwarded?
qa.a: Some might have believed it and felt worried or angry, spreading it further without checking.

grounding: It shows teens questioning a viral political claim and planning to check official sources.

passage: Two weeks before the panchayat election in their village near Nashik, a video began circulating: a candidate standing beside a new school building, captioned 'He built this!' Jeevan, seventeen, watched it three times at the tea stall. Something bothered him. The school looked exactly like the one in the next district. His sister Rashmi, nineteen and voting for the first time, asked, 'So should I vote for him?' 'Let's check first,' Jeevan said. They went to the gram panchayat office and asked to see the list of works done. The school wasn't on it. 'So the video is false?' 'This part is. Doesn't mean he's bad. Just check his real work, and the others' too.' Rashmi nodded and borrowed the list.

qa.q: Where did Jeevan and Rashmi go to check the claim?
qa.a: The gram panchayat office, where they asked for the list of works done.

qa.q: What made Jeevan suspicious of the video?
qa.a: He noticed the school looked like one in the next district, so something felt off.

qa.q: What did Jeevan do well as Rashmi prepared to vote?
qa.a: He checked the claim at the source and kept his conclusion fair, not deciding for her.

qa.q: How might Rashmi approach future campaign videos after this?
qa.a: She might check official records before believing them, as a first-time voter learning how local government works.

grounding: Shows a rural teen checking a political claim and learning how local elections and records work.

passage: In Johannesburg, Lindiwe, seventeen, was reading two news sites about the city council's vote to raise water tariffs. One headline said, 'Council Robs Residents!' The other said, 'Council Approves Tariff Change After Drought Warnings.' She frowned and messaged Sami from civics class: 'Same story, totally different vibe.' Sami replied, 'Check the actual council minutes. They're public.' That evening she found them online. Forty councillors had voted; the reasons were listed, and some had objected. She also found out her ward councillor's name for the first time. Lindiwe turns eighteen next year. She added a reminder on her phone: 'Register to vote.' Then she emailed her councillor a question about the drought plan.

qa.q: What were the two headlines Lindiwe read about the council?
qa.a: 'Council Robs Residents!' and 'Council Approves Tariff Change After Drought Warnings.'

qa.q: How did Lindiwe feel reading the two different headlines?
qa.a: She was puzzled and a bit suspicious, noticing the same story was told with very different emotion.

qa.q: Which of Lindiwe's steps could any young reader copy?
qa.a: Comparing sources, reading the original public record and contacting their representative with a question.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe's councillor see an email from a young resident?
qa.a: The councillor might be pleased, or at least reminded that young future voters are paying attention.

grounding: Shows a teen outside India reading news critically and learning how local governance and voting work.
